shape.name: Shape F - Productive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional productive skills lesson with preparation stages followed by speaking or writing output.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Here the focus is on helping learners practice their speaking or writing skills. The lesson can usually be divided into preparation for speaking/writing and speaking/writing task stages.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to [speak/write] about [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to draft a four-paragraph compare-and-contrast essay from their notes, using linking words, stronger comparisons, and a clear concluding opinion, then review and edit their draft.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
09-08-26
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
F (Productive Skills - Writing)
Materials:
Textbook writing workshop pp. 135-137, slideshow, essay topic cards, essay plans
Assessment:
Drafted and edited essay
Skills:
Writing

stages.stage_aim: To reactivate lessons 1 and 2 and set the theme: today we draft the full essay from our plan
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: "What do you see? Someone writing. What might this lesson be about?" Let students guess.
Advance to the title slide: "Draft it. Polish it." Confirm the theme: today we write the full essay from our plan.
Show the "Why is this lesson important?" slide and read the bullets aloud.
Pairs recap: "What are the four parts of an essay? Which three ideas did you choose?" Students restate their ideas in one sentence.
Point to the Opinion-Reason-Evidence line at the bottom of the slide.

stages.stage_aim: To teach the hook-and-question introduction and draft the opening paragraph
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "The introduction."
Teach the strategy table: ask a question in the first line to hook the reader.
Reveal the Exercise 1 answer: the model essay opens with "But which type of sports are best: team or individual?" and "How do they compare?"
Exercise 2: students write their own introduction from their notes, asking the question and comparing both sides.

stages.stage_aim: To teach contrasting linking words, including conjunctive adverbs after a semicolon, and apply them to the notes
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Link your ideas."
Teach the strategy table: use linking words to contrast; match the word to one sentence or after a semicolon.
Present the key phrases: one-sentence words (although, despite, whereas, while) and after-a-semicolon words (however, nevertheless, even so, on the other hand).
Run the demo: the film sentence with the green checkmark on "however". Stress: semicolon before, comma after, not capitalised.
Reveal the Exercise 3 answers row by row.
Exercise 4: students choose a linking word for each of their own ideas.

stages.stage_aim: To teach stronger comparison phrases and write the two main paragraphs
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Make comparisons stronger."
Present the key phrases: much, far more, far less, nowhere near as.
Run the demo: choose the stronger sentence (far more stimulating).
Exercise 6: students write their second and third paragraphs from their notes. 8 minutes (timer).
Monitor: linking words and comparisons appear in every paragraph.

stages.stage_aim: To teach the opinion-phrase key phrases and write a clear concluding paragraph
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Write your conclusion."
Teach the strategy table: repeat your opinion clearly; summarise one point from each side first.
Reveal the Exercise 8 key phrases: I'd say that ..., It's my opinion that ..., I strongly believe that ..., It's clear that ..., The way I see it, ...
Exercises 7 and 9: students make notes for their conclusion, then write it. 5 minutes (timer).

stages.stage_aim: For students to revise their draft: synonyms, cuts, register, and proofreading
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Review and edit."
Teach the synonym strategy and reveal the Exercise 2 answers (advantages becomes benefits, important becomes valuable, great becomes wonderful).
Teach the cuts strategy and the neutral-words strategy.
Students complete Exercises 1, 3, 4 and 5: check paragraphs, replace repeated words, make cuts, read aloud, and proofread. 8 minutes (timer).

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the completed draft and set the final-copy task
procedure: Show the wrap-up slide: "Your essay is ready."
Exercise 6 on page 137: students write the corrected final copy for homework or in the next class.
Collect the drafts.

shape.note: For middle schoolers interested in SCR approach to productive skills, see Shape J instead.

metadata.topic: Compare and contrast essays: draft, link, and review
materials: Oxford Discover Futures 3, Unit "Writing workshop: A compare and contrast essay", pp. 135–137
Slideshow — Lesson 3: Draft, Link, and Review
Essay topic cards — each student's topic from Lesson 1
Essay plans — each student's notes from Lesson 2
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to draft a four-paragraph compare-and-contrast essay from their notes, using linking words, stronger comparisons, and a clear concluding opinion, then review and edit their draft.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also be better able to contrast ideas using conjunctive adverbs after a semicolon (however, nevertheless) and subordinating conjunctions (although, despite), and to strengthen comparisons with far more, far less, and nowhere near as.
answer_key: The model essay opens with the questions "But which type of sports are best: team or individual?" and "How do they compare?" The introduction presents both sides and asks the question the essay will answer.
1 It can be easy to feel lonely in a city despite the thousands of people who live there.
2 Students don't have much money; nevertheless, they may be able to get a higher-earning job later.
3 Exotic fruit is delicious; however, it often has a high carbon footprint.
4 Housing is cheaper in a village; on the other hand, commuting can cost a lot.
1 I'd say that ... 2 It's my opinion that ... 3 I strongly believe that ... 4 It's clear that ... 5 The way I see it, ...
The model repeats ideas but not words: advantages becomes benefits, important becomes valuable, and great becomes wonderful.
